title: The Rough Riders
subtitle: Cuba, 1898
intro: He resigned a comfortable job in Washington to raise a regiment of cowboys, Ivy League athletes, and lawmen — then took them up a hill in Cuba mostly on foot, because their horses never left Florida. Fifteen questions on the summer that made him famous.

questions.prompt: What was the regiment's official name?
options: The First United States Volunteer Cavalry
questions.explanation: The First United States Volunteer Cavalry. "Rough Riders" was a newspaper coinage, borrowed from Wild West show billing, and the men adopted it because it was better than anything the army came up with.
questions.imageAlt: Roosevelt and the Rough Riders at the top of the captured hill
questions.credit: Colonel Roosevelt and his Rough Riders at the top of the hill which they captured. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: What post did Roosevelt resign in order to go to war?
questions.explanation: Assistant Secretary of the Navy — a job he had wanted badly and had used to push the fleet toward readiness. When war came he resigned to fight in it, against the advice of nearly everyone who liked him.
questions.imageAlt: Roosevelt greeting Colonel Brodie of the Rough Riders
questions.credit: Greeting Col. Brodie of Rough Riders. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: Roosevelt was offered command of the regiment but turned it down. Why?
options: He thought he lacked the military experience and asked for second-in-command
He was too ill to lead
He wanted a naval command instead
questions.explanation: He judged that he did not yet know enough to command a regiment in the field, and asked instead to serve under Leonard Wood, an army surgeon with a Medal of Honor and real campaign experience. Roosevelt took the lieutenant-colonelcy and learned the job. He got the colonelcy later, when Wood was promoted.
questions.imageAlt: Roosevelt greeting Colonel Brodie of the Rough Riders
questions.credit: Greeting Col. Brodie of Rough Riders. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: Where did the regiment muster and train?
questions.explanation: San Antonio, Texas. Wood went ahead to set up the camp; Roosevelt followed on May 12, 1898. The recruits arrived from the territories and the eastern colleges within days of each other, which is roughly as long as they had to become a regiment.
questions.imageAlt: Roosevelt greeting Colonel Brodie of the Rough Riders
questions.credit: Greeting Col. Brodie of Rough Riders. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: Who filled the ranks of the Rough Riders?
options: Regular army cavalry transferred from the frontier
Cowboys and lawmen from the territories alongside Ivy League athletes and clubmen
questions.explanation: Both, deliberately. Roosevelt recruited hunters, cowpunchers, sheriffs and Native American troopers from the western territories, and mixed them with Harvard, Yale and Princeton men — including a polo player or two and an Englishman who turned up expecting cavalrymen to carry canes.
questions.imageAlt: Roosevelt and the Rough Riders on the captured hill
questions.credit: Colonel Roosevelt and his Rough Riders at the top of the hill which they captured. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: What happened to most of the regiment's horses?
options: They were shipped to Cuba with the men
They were left behind in Tampa for lack of transport
They were sold to the Cuban army
questions.explanation: There was not enough shipping. Most of the horses stayed in Tampa, so a cavalry regiment fought its war on foot — as did the rest of the division, cavalry in name only. Officers' horses were allowed aboard, which is why Roosevelt was mounted and conspicuous when the others were not.
questions.imageAlt: Painting of the charge of the Rough Riders at San Juan Hill
questions.credit: Charge of the Rough Riders at San Juan Hill, reproduction of a painting. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: What was the regiment's first fight, on June 24, 1898?
questions.explanation: Las Guásimas, named for a pass about twelve miles from Santiago. The Rough Riders pushed through jungle and heavy undergrowth in brutal heat against entrenched Spanish troops they mostly could not see. It was a shock, and it taught them what smokeless powder meant.
questions.imageAlt: The monument on San Juan Hill
questions.credit: The monument on San Juan Hill. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: On July 1, 1898, which hill did Roosevelt and the Rough Riders actually charge?
questions.explanation: Kettle Hill. The larger action is remembered as San Juan Hill, and the two are part of the same San Juan Heights, but Roosevelt's charge went up Kettle Hill. From the top he had a clear view of Kent's infantry still working their way up San Juan Hill across the valley.
questions.imageAlt: Painting of the charge of the Rough Riders at San Juan Hill
questions.credit: Charge of the Rough Riders at San Juan Hill, reproduction of a painting. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: How was Roosevelt most easily identified during the charge?
options: By a blue polka-dot neckerchief flying from his hat
By carrying the regimental colours himself
questions.explanation: A blue neckerchief with white polka dots, worn round his hat and streaming behind him. His men remembered it for the rest of their lives — "the man with the flying blue neckerchief." It also made him an obvious target, which he seems not to have minded.
questions.imageAlt: Roosevelt and the Rough Riders at the top of the captured hill
questions.credit: Colonel Roosevelt and his Rough Riders at the top of the hill which they captured. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: Which weapon gave decisive support to the American advance on the heights?
questions.explanation: Lieutenant John Parker's Gatling guns opened on the Spanish trenches and their effect on the defenders was immediate. Roosevelt was unstinting about it afterwards, and said so in print — unusual generosity from a man writing his own account of his own battle.
questions.imageAlt: A man at a Gatling gun, from the Roosevelt collection
questions.credit: Lieut. Parker and his Gatlings. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: Roosevelt was recommended for the Medal of Honor in 1898. What happened?
options: It was blocked, and not awarded until long after his death
It was downgraded to a Distinguished Service Cross
questions.explanation: He was recommended for it, and he wanted it badly. The award was blocked — Roosevelt had been publicly scathing about the War Department's handling of the campaign, and the Secretary of War was in no mood to decorate him. It was finally awarded in 2001, posthumously.
questions.imageAlt: The monument on San Juan Hill
questions.credit: The monument on San Juan Hill. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: What did Roosevelt do with the story of the regiment after the war?
options: Wrote a bestselling account called The Rough Riders
Published it only after leaving the presidency
questions.explanation: He wrote The Rough Riders, serialised and then published in 1899. It sold well and it fixed the legend. Finley Peter Dunne's satirical review suggested a more honest title would have been "Alone in Cuba" — a joke Roosevelt enjoyed enough to write and tell Dunne so.
questions.imageAlt: Painting of the charge of the Rough Riders
questions.credit: Charge of the Rough Riders at San Juan Hill, reproduction of a painting. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: What ended the regiment's war, more than Spanish bullets did?
options: Disease — yellow fever and malaria in the camps
questions.explanation: Fever. With Santiago taken, the army sat in a pestilential camp losing men daily to yellow fever and malaria while Washington hesitated to bring them home. Roosevelt helped force the issue with a blunt public letter, which did nothing for his standing at the War Department.
questions.imageAlt: The monument on San Juan Hill
questions.credit: The monument on San Juan Hill. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: How long did the Rough Riders exist as a regiment?
options: Through the whole war and occupation
questions.explanation: Roughly four months, from muster in May 1898 to muster out in September. They trained for weeks, fought for a fortnight, and were disbanded before the leaves turned — and they are remembered better than regiments that served for decades.
questions.imageAlt: Roosevelt and the Rough Riders on the captured hill
questions.credit: Colonel Roosevelt and his Rough Riders at the top of the hill which they captured. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: What did Cuba do for Roosevelt's political career?
options: Very little — he was already famous
It made him a national hero and he was elected Governor of New York within months
It delayed his career by several years
questions.explanation: He came home in August 1898 a national figure and was elected Governor of New York that November. Three years later he was president. The hill in Cuba is where the last stretch of that climb began.

questions.credit: Greeting Col. Brodie of Rough Riders. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.
